Jessica the jackrabbit wants to climb down a wall. The wall consists of 2026 horizontal layers stacked vertically. The $n$th layer from the top is partitioned into $2^n - 1$ identical rectangular bricks arranged side by side. Jessica begins in the topmost layer, which contains a single brick. A move consists of Jessica going down one layer to a brick that shares a side with the brick she is currently on.

Determine, with proof, the total number of distinct sequences of moves Jessica can take to reach the 2026th layer.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let the common width of the wall be scaled to \(1\). Since the \(n\)-th layer has \(2^n-1\) congruent bricks arranged side by side, the \(i\)-th brick in layer \(n\) has horizontal span

\[
I_{n,i}=\left[\frac{i-1}{2^n-1},\frac{i}{2^n-1}\right].
\]

Two bricks in consecutive layers share a side exactly when their horizontal spans overlap in a segment of positive length.

Fix layer \(n\), and set

\[
m=2^n-1.
\]

Then the next layer has

\[
2m+1
\]

bricks. Consider brick \(i\) in layer \(n\), where \(1\le i\le m\). Its span is

\[
[L,R]=\left[\frac{i-1}{m},\frac{i}{m}\right].
\]

The boundaries in layer \(n+1\) occur at multiples of

\[
\frac{1}{2m+1}.
\]

We compare \(L\) and \(R\) to those boundaries. A straightforward algebraic comparison gives

\[
\frac{2i-2}{2m+1}\le \frac{i-1}{m}<\frac{2i-1}{2m+1}
\]

and

\[
\frac{2i}{2m+1}<\frac{i}{m}\le \frac{2i+1}{2m+1}.
\]

The first inequality says that the left endpoint of the brick in layer \(n\) lies in (or at the left edge of) the \((2i-1)\)-st brick of the next layer. The second says that the right endpoint lies in (or at the right edge of) the \((2i+1)\)-st brick of the next layer.

Therefore the brick in layer \(n\) shares a side with exactly the three bricks in layer \(n+1\) numbered

\[
2i-1,\qquad 2i,\qquad 2i+1.
\]

So every brick in every layer except the bottom has exactly \(3\) legal downward moves.

Starting from the single brick in layer \(1\), reaching layer \(2026\) requires exactly \(2025\) moves. Since each move has \(3\) choices, the number of distinct sequences of moves is

\[
\boxed{3^{2025}}.
\]
